title: Radiation from the nucleus

criteria.text: Know that nuclear stability depends on proton to neutron ratios
Understand the roles of the electrostatic force, the strong nuclear force and the weak nuclear force
Know that electrostatic forces on protons in the nucleus are extremely large repulsive forces
Know that the nucleus contains a short-range strong nuclear force that can overcome electrostatic repulsion forces
Know that the weak force explains the transformation of protons into neutrons and vice versa
Know the properties of α-, β⁻-, β⁺- and γ-radiation
Explain nuclear transformations using decay equations involving α-, β⁻-, β⁺- and γ-radiation
Understand the concept of half-life for radioactive sources
Determine the strength (activity) of radioactive sources after a whole number of half-lives have elapsed
Analyse radioactive isotope decay chains (e.g. U-238) and understand that a decay series is a sequence of stages a radioisotope passes through before eventually reaching a stable isotope
Explain effects of α-, β⁻-, β⁺- and γ-radiation on humans
Understand the different capacity of α-, β⁻-, β⁺- and γ-radiation to cause cell damage
Understand the short- and long-term effects of low and high doses of radiation
Understand the ionising impacts of external and internal radiation sources
Be able to calculate absorbed dose (gray), equivalent dose (sievert) and effective dose (sievert)
Evaluate the use of medical radioisotopes in therapy including the effects on healthy and damaged tissues and cells

review_questions.question: The stability of any nucleus depends on the number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. What is the approximate neutron/proton ratio for:
review_questions.answer:
a For small nuclei to be stable, the number of protons must roughly equal the number of neutrons.
b For larger nuclei, as the number of protons increases, more neutrons are needed to maintain nuclear stability at the larger end the ratio is approximately 1.5:1.

review_questions.question:
a What are nucleons?
b Explain how individual nucleons are held together in a nucleus, given that like charges repel.

a All of the protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
b The pull of the strong nuclear force on the nucleons is greater than the electrostatic repulsion of the protons.

review_questions.question:
a How is β⁻-decay of a nucleus possible when a nucleus does not contain any electrons?
b How is β⁺-decay of a nucleus possible when a nucleus does not contain any positrons?
review_questions.answer:
a A neutron turns into a proton and emits an electron (β⁻): $^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow {}^{1}_{1}\text{p} + {}^{0}_{-1}\text{e}$
b A proton turns into a neutron emitting a positron or beta-plus particle (β⁺): $^{1}_{1}\text{p} \rightarrow {}^{1}_{0}\text{n} + {}^{0}_{+1}\text{e}$

review_questions.answer:
a The half-life is the time taken for half of a group of unstable nuclei to decay.
b The activity is the number of radioactive nuclei that decay each second, measured in bequerel (Bq).
c 13.5 billion years
n = 3 half-lives as $\frac{50}{400} = \frac{1}{8} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3}$ (4.5 billion years × 3)

review_questions.question: Radioactive isotopes are used for both diagnostic and treatment purposes in medicine.
review_questions.answer:
a Low activity (minimise radiation damage), short half-life (don't linger in the patient), low ionisation (minimise radiation damage) and good penetration (can escape the body and can be seen using γ-ray cameras).
b High activity (maximise damage to cancerous cells), long half-life (no need to replace hospital radiotherapy units too often), low ionisation (minimise radiation damage to healthy surrounding cells) and good penetration (can travel through the body to the spot where the beams are all concentrated).

parts.question: Explain some of the characteristics needed for γ-ray radioisotopes used for medical diagnostic purposes.
parts.answer: Low activity (minimise radiation damage), short half-life (don't linger in the patient), low ionisation (minimise radiation damage) and good penetration (can escape the body and can be seen using γ-ray cameras).

parts.question: Explain some of the characteristics needed for γ-ray radioisotopes used for external medical treatment of malignant cancers.
parts.answer: High activity (maximise damage to cancerous cells), long half-life (no need to replace hospital radiotherapy units too often), low ionisation (minimise radiation damage to healthy surrounding cells) and good penetration (can travel through the body to the spot where the beams are all concentrated).

review_questions.question:
A patient has a 20 g cancerous tumour, which absorbs 0.006 J of energy from an external cobalt-60 γ-emitter radiotherapy unit.
(c, d) Another patient with advanced prostate cancer has a 40 g cancerous tumour, which absorbs 0.004 J of energy from internally implanted radium-223 α-emitting pellets.
review_questions.answer:
a Absorbed dose = $\frac{\text{energy}}{\text{mass}} = \frac{0.006}{0.02}$ = 0.02 J $kg^{-1}$ = 0.30 Gy

c Absorbed dose = $\frac{\text{energy}}{\text{mass}} = \frac{0.004}{0.04}$ = 0.01 J $kg^{-1}$ = 0.10 Gy
d Dose equivalent = absorbed dose × radiation weighting factor = 0.10 × 20 = 2.0 Sv

review_questions.question:
a Why are none of our senses useful in detecting radiation?
b What is the difference between using a Geiger counter or an OLP dosimeter for measuring radiation exposure?
review_questions.answer:
a For 99% of radioactive sources that most people come into contact with, you can't see, smell, taste or hear them, or know that they are radioactive by touching them. Note however that some radioactive sources glow in the dark.
b The Geiger counter gives you an immediate reading of the activity, the film badge dosimeter tells you the amount of radiation you have been exposed to over a certain time interval.

review_questions.question: What is the difference between the somatic effects and genetic effects of ionising radiation?
review_questions.answer: Genetic effects are those that occur in the descendants of a parent whose DNA molecules are modified due to exposure to ionising radiation. Somatic effects are those that occur in the exposed individual including damage that is caused to the chromosomes in individual body tissue cells.

review_questions.question: Ionising radiation creates ions such as $OH^{-}$ and $H^{+}$. Why are these ions dangerous for humans?
review_questions.answer: The ions are chemically reactive and can cause cell damage, disturb the regulation of cell reproduction and even cause cell death.

review_questions.question: In external beam radiotherapy, why are there a large number of low-dose beams aimed at a brain tumour from different angles rather than just a single, fixed, high-dose beam of radiation from only one angle? You should use the diagram below in your explanation. The brain tumour is shown in yellow.
review_questions.answer: The radiotherapy equipment focuses many small beams of radiation on the tumour. Each beam has very little effect on the healthy tissue it passes through, but a targeted dose of radiation of high intensity is delivered to the site where all the beams intersect.

summary:
Chapter 3 Summary

3A Nuclear stability: forces in the nucleus

-   Nuclear model atom: electrons circulate about a nucleus of neutrons and protons. Number of protons defines each element.

-   Artificial elements with more than 92 protons are unstable.

-   Nucleon: a proton or a neutron in a nucleus.

-   Nucleus: the solid centre of an atom where most of the mass of an atom is concentrated.

-   Proton: a positively charged particle in the nucleus of an atom.

-   Element: a pure substance consisting only of atoms that all have the same numbers of protons in their nuclei.

-   Neutron: an uncharged particle in the nucleus of an atom.

-   Z = symbol for atomic number = count of protons in an element.

-   A = symbol for atomic mass = number of protons and neutrons.

-   Periodic Table displays elements in a periodic way depending on chemical properties of elements.

-   Convention is to display element with symbol X as AXZ.

-   Isotope is a form of the same element with the same numbers of protons but different numbers of neutrons in their nuclei.

-   Radioactive Isotope any isotope of an element whose nuclei are unstable and dissipate energy by spontaneously emitting radiation.

-   In nuclear physics, radiation is a group-name for any radiated particle or energy, including electromagnetic radiation and electrons, for example.

-   Some radiation is useful in medicine to target cancerous cells (e.g.in tumours).

-   Nuclear stability depends on ratio of number of neutrons to protons: about 1:1 for elements with Z up to about 20; increasing to 1.4 for Z = 50; and to 1.5 for Z = 80.

-   More neutrons are needed to maintain stability for large number of protons to moderate the competing electrostatic force and the strong nuclear force in the nucleus.

-   In the nucleus, between protons electrostatic forces are extremely large, repulsive forces.

-   Four fundamental forces: gravitational, weak nuclear, electromagnetic (a.k.a. electrostatic), and the strong nuclear.

-   The short-range strong nuclear force overcomes electrostatic repulsion forces between protons.

-   The weak force explains the transformation of neutrons into protons with emission of negative beta particle (i.e. an electron), and vice versa (i.e. protons into neutrons with emission of positive beta).

> [image]

[image]

-   Binding energy is the amount of energy required to reverse the original process of binding the nucleons in the nucleus.

-   Putting a proton and neutron together to create a Hydrogen nucleus would release 2.23 MeV of energy (and the nucleus would have less mass than the sum of the p and n by an amount m = E/c^2

-   Binding energy per nucleon is a measure of stability for atoms of elements of larger number of nucleons.

-   Iron (Fe) is most stable (has highest binding energy per nucleon); elements up to Fe created in stars. Elements with nucleons greater than that of Fe must be created in cosmic events of greater energy than fusion in stars.

3B Alpha, beta and gamma radiation

-   α (helium nuclei), β-- (electrons), β+ (positrons) and γ-radiation (electromagnetic energy) the first three decay-products discovered) have different penetrating power.

[image]

-   α (due to mass and speed) is a very strong ionising agent of anything within close range.

-   Decay equations for nuclear transformations:

[image]

[image]

[image]

-   Beta carries a range of energies, and decay by beta is accompanied by emission of a neutrino (so total energy of reaction is conserved).

-   Alpha particles have a specific energy for each element.

-   Gamma rays have smaller amount of energy but due to greater penetrating power are dangerous even at a distance.

-   Nuclear transformation is conversion of a nuclide into another (as above for Uranium to Thorium) and below:

> [image]

-   After emission of alpha or beta, nucleons re-arrange to lower energy-state, and emit gamma.

-   In each equation note conservation of Mass Number (superscript on each symbol) on each side of equation, and of Atomic Number (subscript on each symbol).

3C Modelling radioactive decay

-   Radioactive decay of any one nucleus is random (i.e. unpredictable).

-   Half-life is the time taken, on average, for the decay of half of the nuclei in a large sample of radioactive nuclei (so is also the time for radioactivity to be halved).

-   Because decay-rate depends on number of nucleons, mathematically N = N_0(1/2)^n is an exponential curve (N = number now, N_0 = original number, n = number of half-lives).

-   For medical uses, need an isotope that has a short half-life (so it passes quickly through a body).

-   Activity (a.k.a. strength) of decay is rate of decay: unit -- becquerel (Bq) = 1 decay per second.

-   Radiocarbon dating is a method for determining the age of an object that contains organic material by using the decay of radioactive carbon-14 (the date being that of the death of the organic matter).

3D Analysing decay series diagrams

-   Radioactive isotope decay chains (e.g. U-238) produce intermediate radioactive products (also known as daughter products) until a final stable element (e.g. lead) is reached.

-   Elements in the chain are called a family, also known as series.

-   For decay by electron emission, the daughter will have a higher Atomic Number.

3E The effect of radiation on humans

-   α, β--, β+ and γ-radiation ionise atoms and within cells in a body that is dangerous especially to cell-division.

-   Cells that are damaged but survive unrepaired may lead to cancer.

-   The different capacity of α, β--, β+ and γ-radiation to cause cell damage depends on penetrating power, and energy.

[image]

-   Absorbed dose is the amount of energy absorbed by each kilogram of tissue that is irradiated; measured in grays (Gy).

-   Gray (Gy) the SI unit of the absorbed dose of ionising radiation, corresponding to 1 J kg^--1

-   Sievert (Sv) the SI unit of dose equivalent (the biological effect of ionising radiation), equal to an effective dose of a joule of energy per kilogram of recipient mass.

-   Ionisations in a cell for a given dose of radiation are much greater for alpha than for beta or gamma, so a weighting factor is applied.

-   Dose equivalent dose equivalent (Sv) = absorbed dose (Gy) × radiation weighting factor.

-   Radiation weighting factor a factor by which the absorbed dose (Gy) is to be multiplied to obtain a quantity that expresses, on a common scale for all ionising radiation, the biological damage (Sv) to an exposed individual.

-   Weighting factors differs for diverse body-parts.

-   Genetic effects uncertain: 2 types = chromosomal aberration (i.e. changes in number or structure of chromosomes) and genetic mutations (i.e. altering sequence in a gene).

-   Radiotherapy a strategy to target cancerous tumours with maximum effect by using large doses of lethal (to the targeted cells) radiation while minimising collateral damage to healthy cells.
